Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The proposed project area is situated primarily
within the boundaries of a sagebrush treatment located approximately 20 miles south 0f
Bloomfield, New Mexico. The brush treatment in question consisted of applying the
herbicide Tebuthiuron to 1,927 acres of rangeland (see map 2) dominated by Wyoming
big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata wyominensis) during the fall of 1993. This area
provides important habitat for big game species such as pronghorn antelope (Antilocapra
Americana) and a host of other lesser mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians. In
keeping with the management objectives of the Farmington Field Office&$s Pronghorn
Antelope Management Plan (BLM 2005) justification for the Proposed Action will be
based upon attaining the following resource goals which in tum will reduce habitat
deficiencies identified for antelope. These goals are:
1. Increase the production of herbaceous plants (primarily forbs) by at least 50
percent. Improved herbaceous plant production will provide additional
protein (which is essential to milk production) to mammals, especially large
ungulates, during the spring/summer when it is needed by lactating females.
2. Create a mosaic of uneven age shrubs (Wyoming big sagebrush - Artemisia
tridentata wyomingensis) of varying heights, densities and canopy coverage&$s.
In particular it is desired that adequate sagebrush remain for fall/winter forage
and antelope fawning cover. Sage as well as herbaceous cover should range
in height from 11 to 25 inches for optimal habitat suitability (BLM, 1980:
Autenrieth, 1984). Because the burn would be patchy, there would obviously
be areas where the cover would be much higher or lower than this amount.
3. Create an interspersion of vegetative types (i.e. grasses, forbs, shrubs) that
will enhance the faunal diversity at various trophic levels, e.g., increased
herbaceous vegetation will increase the productivity of primary producers
such as invertebrates and small mammals which in tum will benefit secondary
consumers such as coyotes (Canis latrans) and red-tailed hawks (Buteo
jamaicensis).

Objectives:
The proposed action would restore ecosystem structure and function to ponderosa pine forests
within the Mount Trumbull Resource Conservation Area. Implementation of the proposed action
would help develop the scientific basis for the restoration of ecological health to portions of
\xb7 southwestern ponderosa pine forests. Furthermore, the proposed action would respond to the
need to test scientific hypotheses regarding the restoration of structure and function in ponderosa
pine forests
Planned_Implementation:
Slash would be removed from site, piled and burned on site, or broadcast throughout the site
and then burned. In all cases where practical, the majority of slash in restoration units would not
be accumulated into piles for burning. Where piling is absolutely necessary, piles of slash would
be placed in bare areas away from leave trees. Bare areas with high cinder content in the soil are
preferable, due to their lack of vegetation growth. When piling in bare areas is not possible,
precautions would be taken in the accumulation of slash piles to minimize excessive soil heating
and potential "soil sterilization.&& Timely burning of slash (under prescription at the earliest
possible date) would reduce the potential for bark beetle outbreaks.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The primary purpose of this project is to reduce the incidence of crown fires on BLM lands
adjacent to private properties between Kerber Creek and Noland Gulch. Secondly, this project
will improve winter big game habitat. The Noland Gulch Fuels Reduction Project is a proposal
to initially mechanically convert approximately 1100 acres of predominantly pinion/juniper
woodland to open woodland (savannah type) with a grass/forb understory. Following this initial
mechanical treatment 600 acres will be treated for prescribed fire if conditions permit. The area
would serve as wildfire fuel breaks to reduce crown fires and rates of spread while giving fire
fighters more suppression opportunities as well as safety routes. The proposed action is to
initially use mechanical treatment in the pinion/juniper woodlands to reduce fuel loads.
Mechanical treatment could include on or all of the following: hydro-axe chipping, horizontal
chipping (Fecon flail type), roller chopping, chain saws, etc. Once fuel loads are reduced,
prescribed fire would be utilized to maintain the treated area. Treatment areas would be confined
to 30% or less slopes to reduce soil erosion. In areas where hand thinning is required, the
resulting slash piles would be burned when weather and environmental conditions permit.
Treatments would be designed to leave a natural appearance while reducing fire spread risk (no
straight edges).

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Proposed Action: to implement a prescribed fire program in Upper Rio Puerco watershed will require
continuous fine fuels to be established and maintained through proper grazing use and deferred grazing of
rangelands prior to ignition. Stubble heights (residual vegetation) is required to facilitate a prescribed fire program
within big sagebrush communities. To accomplish this the proposed action will incorporate standards for grazing
deferment pre- and post- burn, see Section 3.13 and Appendix No. 2 Special Conditions for Prescribed Fire
Cooperative Agreements. In addition the proposed action will use rangeland indicators to determine the Appropriate
Conditions to Use Fire as presented in Section 3.12.
The resource objectives of the proposed action is to maintain watersheds in healthy condition and to improve the
rangelands soil stability, biotic diversity and hydrologic function. Implementation of prescribed fire on rangelands
to fulfill these objectives may require a fire cycle of every six to eight (6 - 8) years. The actual fire cycle, however,
will be determined through the use of rangeland indicators to determine the Appropriate Conditions to Use Fire as
presented in Section 3.12.

The Chain of Craters Prescribed fire is within the El Malpais National
Conservation Area and the Chain of Craters Wilderness Study Area. This project is located
approximately 30 miles southwest of Grants on the Cerro Brillante Quadrangle in T8N, R13W, Sections
20, 21, 27,28,29,30, 31, 32, 33, & 34&* T7N, R13W, Sections?, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 28, 29,
30, 31, 32, 33, & 34. The project area consists of 14,520 acres (see burn area description) of ponderosa
pine, pin yon, juniper, grass, and brush. This is a hazardous fuels reduction and SYKES Act project. The
goal of this project is to employ management ignited prescribed fire in the pinyon, juniper, and ponderosa
pine to reduce stand densities, ladder fuels, and hazardous fuel loadings that contribute to the decline of
wildlife habitat and the potential of catastrophic wildfire.
